<reason>Both sides built tight, well-structured cases and sustained real clash across rounds, but B edged the exchange on two fronts. First, B better resolved the "invisible to inspectors vs. reviewable logs" tension A raised in Pressure Questions, distinguishing enemy-facing unverifiability from internal court-facing reviewability — a distinction A's closing simply reasserted as unresolved rather than directly countering. Second, and more decisively, B's own pressure question forced A to explicitly state that accountability should be preserved even if constrained autonomy produced fewer civilian deaths; B's closing crystallized this admission into the debate's most memorable and damaging frame ("keep human control even if more civilians die"), and A's closing never directly re-engaged that tradeoff, instead pivoting back to the "who chose this victim" framing. A's structural point about category-authorization versus individualized victim selection remained the strongest under-rebutted thread in the debate and kept A competitive, but B's tighter use of concrete existing-practice analogies (minefields, BVR missiles, point defense) and its sharper closing exploitation of A's own concession gave B the cleaner final path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Question ("would you still ban it even if audited data showed fewer civilian deaths?") and A's honest but costly answer that accountability outweighs the tradeoff, which B then weaponized in its closing as the decisive concession of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
